theme: Sing to the LORD a new song
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 96. Where yesterday’s psalm warned, today’s celebrates. Read it as a missionary song, and notice how many times it speaks of “all the earth,” “the nations,” and “the peoples.”
settingTheScene: Psalm 96 is closely related to a song of David recorded in 1 Chronicles 16, sung when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. It begins with the call to “sing to the LORD a new song,” and it widens quickly to include the whole world. In the context of Numbers, with its story of a people who failed in unbelief, the psalm lifts the eyes toward a future in which every nation praises the LORD.
observation: “Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth!” (v. 1).
“Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day” (v. 2).
“Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!” (v. 3).
“For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods” (v. 4).
“For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens” (v. 5).
“Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!” (v. 7).
“Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!” (v. 9).
“Say among the nations, The LORD reigns!… He will judge the peoples with equity” (vv. 10-13).
interpretation:
This psalm is a call to worship that is also a call to mission. The singing is not meant to stay in Israel. It is to be declared “among the nations.” The salvation of the LORD is to be told “from day to day.” The God of Israel is not a tribal god. He made the heavens, and he is the only true God.

The “new song” is the response to a new act of salvation. Each generation has to sing for itself what God has done. It is not enough to repeat the old songs only as history. We need to make them new by remembering and applying them to our own situation.

The contrast between the LORD and the gods of the peoples is sharp. Verse 5 uses a Hebrew pun: the word for “idols” sounds like the word for “nothings.” The gods of the nations are worthless things, and the LORD made the heavens. This is the same contrast Israel had just ignored in the wilderness. The psalm urges the nations to turn from nothing to everything.

The psalm ends with creation joining in. The heavens, the earth, the sea, the fields, and the trees of the forest all rejoice, because the LORD is coming to judge the earth. The coming of God is good news for the world. He will judge with equity and truth. In a world full of injustice, this is a hope worth singing about.

After reading about Israel’s complaining, the psalm is a rebuke and an invitation. Israel’s calling was to sing, to witness, and to bring the nations in. The failure of the wilderness is not the end of the story. God will still be praised in all the earth.
connection: Jesus sent his disciples to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). Revelation 5:9 and 7:9 show a multitude from every nation praising the Lamb, singing a “new song.” Paul says that creation “will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21). The coming of the Lord to judge the earth is the Christian’s hope (Acts 17:31; Revelation 19).
application:
Sing or read this psalm aloud. Ask God to give you a new song for something he has done recently.

Pray for a missionary or a nation that has not heard the gospel.

Tell someone this week about something God has done for you.
prayerPrompts: Sing or speak to the LORD a new song, in your own words.
Ask him to make you bold to tell of his salvation.
Pray “Come, Lord Jesus” to judge the earth in righteousness.
